parts.problem_md: Explain **one** method of water transfer in the hydrological cycle.
parts.solution_md:
Evaporation is a method of water transfer **[1]**. Heat energy causes water to change from water  to  steam,  which rises and forms clouds **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**

parts.problem_md: Explain **one** way temperature can affect river regimes
parts.solution_md:
Higher temperatures increase evaporation **[1]**, which reduces discharge** [1]**.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> The command word '**explain**' means that the answer should provide a reasoned outline of why temperature changes affect the discharge in rivers.
> 
> **Mark allocation**
> 
> - One mark **[1] **is awarded for a reason that temperature affects discharge [AO1]
> - One mark **[1] **is awarded for explaining how this affects discharge. [AO2]
> 
> **Alternative content**
>

> - Increased precipitation in winter
> - Freezing temperatures mean snow does not melt

parts.problem_md:
Study** Figure 2**, a flood hydrograph showing river discharge following a period of heavy rainfall.

![Graph showing precipitation as beige bars and discharge as a blue line. Discharge peaks at 10-12 hours after storm, while precipitation ends by 10 hours.](assets/001-graph-showing-precipitation-as-beige-bars-and-di.png)

Using **Figure 2**, describe the changes in river discharge shown.
parts.solution_md:
After 1 hour of the storm, the discharge was just under 25 cumecs. **[1]** The discharge then rose quickly, reaching a peak of 200 cumecs at approximately 11 hours after rainfall began. **[1]** After the peak, discharge fell  gradually over the remaining hours, dropping to around 22 cumecs by hour 21 and returning to its base flow. **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> The command word '**describe**' means that the answer needs to state what the graph shows, **using data from Figure 2** where possible. No explanation of why changes occur is required.
> 
> **Mark allocation**
> 
> This answer is assessed using a** point-marked** approach.
> 
> - **One mark **for each valid descriptive point, using data from Figure 2, up to a maximum of 3 marks
> 
> **[3 marks]**
> 
> **Alternative content**
> 
> The answer above is just one example of how to respond to this question. Alternative information that could be provided in the answer includes:
> 
> - Reference to the lag time, if clearly identified from the figure
> - Description of the overall shape of the hydrograph as having a short lag time
> - Any other appropriate response
> 
> **Common errors**
> 
> - Explaining the causes of the hydrograph shape [for example, referring to impermeable rock or urbanisation] rather than describing what the graph shows
> - Describing only one feature of the graph, such as the peak, and miss the rising limb, falling limb, and base flow
> - Failing to quote any data values from the figure; using figures from the graph is expected and gains credit

> **[exam-tip]**
> **For** 'describe the changes' questions using a graph, always work from left to right: start at the beginning, describe what happens in the middle, and finish at the end.
> 
> **Aim** for three separate observations to match the three marks available. Data equals marks; if a value appears on the graph, use it.
> 
> **Examiners** want to see that you can read a graph accurately, so quote specific numbers wherever you can.

parts.problem_md: Explain why deforestation in a drainage basin can increase the risk of flooding.
parts.solution_md:
When trees are removed, there is less interception of rainfall, so more water reaches the ground surface directly. **[1]** Without tree roots to absorb water, the soil becomes saturated more quickly, which increases surface run-off and overland flow. **[1]** This means water enters the river much faster, causing discharge to rise rapidly and significantly increasing the risk of a flood. **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> The command word **'explain why**' means that the answer needs to provide reasons and show understanding of cause and effect. Describing what deforestation is will not be sufficient on its own.
> 
> **Mark allocation**
> 
> This answer is assessed using a **point-marked** approach.
> 
> - **One mark** for a valid point
> - **One mark** for development of a point
> 
> **[3 marks]**
> 
> **Alternative content**
> 
> The answer above is just one example of how to respond to this question. Alternative information that could be provided in the answer includes:
> 
> - Reference to the water cycle or hydrological cycle terminology such as throughflow, infiltration, and percolation
> - Reference to reduced evapotranspiration as a consequence of tree removal
> - Any other appropriate response
> 
> **Common errors**
> 
> - Stating 'there are fewer trees to absorb water' but do not complete the chain of reasoning to explain what happens next; the explanation must be developed through to the flood risk
> - Confusing interception [trees catching rainfall on their leaves and branches] with absorption [roots taking in water from the soil]
> - Writing about the physical appearance of a deforested landscape rather than the hydrological consequences

parts.problem_md:
Study Figure 1c below

Analyse the factors that affect the river regime shown in figure 1c

![screenshot-2023-08-15-at-10-11-53](assets/005-screenshot-2023-08-15-at-10-11-53.png)
parts.solution_md:
The river regime in Figure 1c is influenced by both the physical features and the land uses in the drainage basin. A river regime means how the discharge changes over time. At gauging station A, the hydrograph is much “flashier”, with a high peak discharge of around 70 cumecs and a short lag time **[S]**. This is because the river there flows through an urban area (shown in grey on Figure 1c), where impermeable surfaces like roads stop infiltration and increase surface run-off **[Ap]**. Water reaches the channel quickly, so discharge rises sharply after the storm.

In contrast, gauging station B shows a much lower peak discharge and a longer lag time** [S]**. This part of the basin has more forested land, shown by the tree symbols. Trees intercept rainfall and encourage infiltration, so the water travels more slowly to the river **[Ap]**. There is also pastoral farming upstream, which usually allows more infiltration than urban land, reducing run-off and slowing the response to rainfall** [S]**.

Because the drainage basin includes many tributaries flowing through different land uses, the rivers react differently to the same storm **[Ap][S]**. Overall, Figure 1c shows that human land use, like urbanisation, creates rapid changes in discharge, while natural vegetation leads to a calmer, slower river regime with a delayed peak **[Ap][S].**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> The command word **‘analyse**’ means that the answer needs to break down the components and make evidence-based connections about causes and effects or relationships between them.
> 
> **Mark allocation**
> 
> This answer is assessed using a **'level of response'** approach. Each point made in the answer does not equal a mark.
> 
> The AO focus includes AO3 Analysis **[Ap]** and AO4 Skills. **[S]**
> 
> - A top-level 3 answer ** ****[8 marks]** will include specific examples that show:
> 
>   - Application of knowledge and understanding
>   - Interpretation, analysis and evaluation of geographical information/issues
>   - Judgements supported by evidence
>   - Selection of information, skills and techniques
> 
> **Alternative content**
> 
> The answer above is just one example of how to respond to this question. Alternative information that could be included in the answer includes:
> 
> - Impact of vegetation on lag time
> - Other human interventions such as sewers, dams and water abstraction
> - Shapes of the hydrographs
